title: How should Australian health services credential clinicians and define their scope of practice?
description: What NSQHS Actions 1.23 and 1.24 and the May 2026 ACSQHC credentialing guidance require: who to credential, 3 to 5 year cycles and committee evidence.
shortAnswer: Australian health services accredited to the NSQHS Standards must credential clinicians where relevant and define, monitor and review each clinician's scope of clinical practice (Actions 1.23 and 1.24). The Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care's May 2026 guidance sets a risk-based approach: verify credentials before a clinician starts, decide scope through a Credentialing Committee, re-credential every 3 to 5 years, and limit temporary approvals to about three months.
keyTakeaways: Action 1.24 of the NSQHS Clinical Governance Standard requires processes to ensure clinicians are credentialed, where relevant, and to monitor and improve the effectiveness of the credentialing process.
Action 1.23 requires scope of clinical practice to be defined, monitored, and reviewed periodically and whenever a new service, procedure or technology is introduced or substantially altered.

The ACSQHC published updated guidance, Credentialing and defining scope of practice: Guidance for health services and clinicians, on May 28, 2026. It is guidance that supports the Standards, not a separate statute.
The guidance says re-credentialing should occur every 3 to 5 years, temporary credentialing should generally last up to three months, and verbal emergency approval may cover up to 24 hours.
Credentialing is an assessment of qualifications, experience and performance, so the evidence trail matters as much as training completions.
jurisdiction: Australia (national, applied through state and territory health regulators)
regulator: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC)
appliesTo: Public and private hospitals and day procedure services assessed against the NSQHS Standards
Governing bodies, executives and Credentialing Committee members
Senior medical and dental practitioners, nurse practitioners, endorsed midwives, paramedics and allied health professionals whom a health service or jurisdiction requires to be credentialed
Locums, agency, telehealth and contracted clinicians working under temporary or third party arrangements

sections.heading: What do NSQHS Actions 1.23 and 1.24 require?

blocks.text: Together, Actions 1.23 and 1.24 require a health service to decide what each clinician may do in its facilities, to check that they have the qualifications, experience and skills to do it, and to keep both decisions under review. They sit in the Clinical Governance Standard of the National Safety and Quality Health Service (NSQHS) Standards, second edition, which the [ACSQHC publishes online](https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/national-standards/nsqhs-standards/clinical-governance-standard).

Action 1.24 states that the health service organisation "Conducts processes to ensure that clinicians are credentialed, where relevant" and "Monitors and improves the effectiveness of the credentialing process". Its stated intent is that "A formal process is used to ensure that clinicians have the appropriate qualifications, experience and skills to fulfil their delegated roles and responsibilities." The key tasks are to document credentialing processes in policies, procedures or protocols, and to review audit and system evaluation results for compliance with them.

Action 1.23 requires processes to define scope of clinical practice considering the organization's clinical service capacity and clinical services plan, to monitor that clinicians operate within their designated scope, and to review scope periodically and whenever a new clinical service, procedure or technology is introduced or substantially altered. Action 1.26 adds supervision, including for clinicians who are expanding their scope. Broader workforce training under Actions 1.19 to 1.22 is covered on the [NSQHS Standards workforce training](/regulations/nsqhs-standards-workforce-training) page; this page deals only with credentialing and scope.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects the NSQHS Standards (second edition) and ACSQHC guidance as at November 2026. The ACSQHC is developing a third edition, and says the six foundations of its 2026 National Model for Clinical Governance will form the structure of the next clinical governance standard. Action numbers may change when that edition is released.

sections.heading: What is the 2026 national credentialing guidance?

blocks.text: The current national reference is Credentialing and defining scope of practice: Guidance for health services and clinicians, published by the ACSQHC in May 2026 (ISBN 978-1-923353-49-7). The Commission announced it on May 28, 2026, describing it as [updated national guidance](https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/news-and-media/latest-news/updated-national-guidance-credentialing-and-defining-scope-clinical-practice) that "strengthens the process for credentialing, recredentialing and defining scope of clinical practice" and "promotes a risk-based approach for identifying which clinicians should be credentialed".

The [guidance document](https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/resources/credentialing-and-defining-scope-practice-guidance-health-services-and-clinicians) applies to public and private health services. It supports the Clinical Governance Standard and the [National Model for Clinical Governance](https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/news-and-media/latest-news/introducing-national-model-clinical-governance), released on June 2, 2026 to replace the 2017 National Model Clinical Governance Framework. The Commission says the guidance was informed by the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (Ahpra), National Boards, colleges and specialty societies, states and territories, and private health service providers.

The guidance is not legislation. Its force comes from accreditation: assessors test Action 1.24 against a service's documented process, and many state and territory health departments set their own credentialing policies that the guidance tells services to follow. Where a jurisdiction's policy is more specific, for example on re-credentialing frequency or committee membership, the jurisdiction's policy applies.
The health service decides, using a risk assessment, though some jurisdictions mandate credentialing for particular groups. The guidance says clinicians who need to be credentialed include those who:

items: work independently where there is no effective oversight or supervision from a senior colleague and the care could result in patient harm
perform specific high-risk procedures or interventions beyond the skills covered in their basic training, for which they have had further specialty training
may be required to perform tasks in emergency, temporary or specific contexts

blocks.text: It notes that, in general, jurisdictions already require credentialing for allied health professionals, endorsed midwives, nurse practitioners, paramedics and senior medical and dental practitioners, and that the number of credentialed groups is growing as profession-specific scopes change. It also separates two ideas: a clinician's profession-specific scope comes from their education and registration, while a facility-specific scope is what the service approves them to do at a named site, based on service need, facility capacity and the clinician's credentials. One clinician can hold different scopes at different facilities.

sections.heading: What does a credentialing application have to verify?

blocks.text: The Credentialing Committee verifies qualifications, registration, insurance, history and performance before the clinician starts. The guidance says initial credentialing should be conducted before a clinician commences work, and lists the applicant information the committee should verify and consider:

items: qualifications and formal training documentation, with extra steps for clinicians trained overseas
health practitioner registration details, including any conditions or undertakings
proof of annual professional indemnity insurance
declarations and proof of identity, including a curriculum vitae explaining service gaps longer than 12 months
clinical references and referee checks, and previous and recent clinical experience and performance
active participation in clinical and performance review processes, and the results of a web search relevant to professional role and history

blocks.text: Continuing professional development (CPD) is part of the picture but not the whole of it. The guidance says National Boards, associations and colleges set CPD standards, and that an organization "can set specific CPD requirements related to the role and scope of practice of its credentialed clinicians and should keep evidence of compliance". The registration side of CPD is explained on the [Ahpra CPD registration standards](/regulations/ahpra-cpd-registration-standards) page. On screening, the guidance notes that clinicians in subsidized aged care need a police certificate not more than three years old and that NDIS registered providers require an NDIS Worker Screening Clearance, which links credentialing to the [Aged Care Act worker screening rules](/regulations/aged-care-act-2024-worker-obligations).

sections.heading: Who sits on the Credentialing Committee and what must it do?

blocks.text: The health service must establish one or more Credentialing Committees with written terms of reference, and the governing body must regularly review reports on how well the process works. The guidance says membership should align with state and territory requirements and should include:

items: a clinician who practices in the clinical field relevant to the scope being assessed
an experienced clinician from the relevant college, association or professional body
an experienced human resource professional, or access to one

blocks.text: The guidance also expects committee members to be oriented before they sit. Orientation should cover their role, privacy, security, record keeping and conflict of interest obligations, the credentialing policies, and how to assess and verify applications. That is a training requirement in its own right, and one that many services do not record. The guidance expects committee decisions to be consistent with community expectations and strong enough to withstand external oversight and review, and the service must have review and appeal processes.

sections.heading: How often must clinicians be re-credentialed, and what about temporary approvals?

blocks.text: Re-credentialing should occur every 3 to 5 years, as specified by the relevant jurisdiction, and must be completed before the current credentialing period expires. The guidance adds triggers for earlier review: poor performance, changes in cognitive or physical functioning, decreased clinical volume, a notice from Ahpra about action under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law, a request to change scope, or concerns raised through morbidity and mortality meetings, incidents or complaints.

blocks.text: Two records do most of the work: an expiry register showing every credentialed clinician's current period and scope, and minutes that show each decision was made by a properly constituted committee. The guide on [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) covers how to structure registers so they can be produced at short notice, and [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency) explains how observed competence can support a request to expand scope.

sections.heading: How does credentialing connect to training and competence?

blocks.text: Credentialing decides whether a clinician may do something; training and supervision are how the service supports them to keep doing it safely or to extend what they do. The guidance says clinicians re-credentialing in a specific area should provide evidence of performance review and professional development specific to that area, and comply with training and CPD recommended in college credentialing guidance.

It also says clinicians should not be credentialed for new procedures or technologies until the health service has approved their use, and that the service, not the committee, decides whether to introduce them. In practice that means a training plan for a new procedure should be linked to the service approval and to the scope change, so that supervised cases, competency sign off and the committee decision appear in one record. The [training matrix guide](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) shows one way to hold that link for each role.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry represents each scope item, the credential that supports it and the competence evidence behind it as linked records, so a change to a procedure or a re-credentialing trigger shows which clinicians and which assessments are affected. Health services can see the approach on the [healthcare and life sciences](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences) page.

faqs.q: Is credentialing a legal requirement in Australia?
faqs.a: Not under a single national statute. The obligation comes through NSQHS Action 1.24, which accreditation assessors test, and through state and territory health department policies. The ACSQHC's May 2026 guidance explains how to meet the Action but defers to jurisdictional policy where it is more specific.

No. Registration with a National Board through Ahpra sets the profession-specific scope a clinician may practice anywhere. Credentialing is the health service's own decision about what that clinician may do in its facilities, based on its capability and the clinician's verified experience and performance.

faqs.q: Can one hospital rely on another hospital's credentialing?
faqs.a: Only under a written mutual recognition agreement, and only for credentials. The guidance says the receiving organization should satisfy itself that the other process meets its own criteria, may ask for a Letter of Good Standing, and must still determine scope of practice at its own site.

faqs.q: Do nurses need to be credentialed?
faqs.a: It depends on role and risk. The guidance names nurse practitioners and endorsed midwives among groups jurisdictions generally require to be credentialed, and says services should credential any clinician working without effective supervision or performing high-risk procedures beyond basic training.

faqs.q: What happens to credentialing when the NSQHS third edition arrives?
faqs.a: The ACSQHC says the six foundations of its 2026 National Model for Clinical Governance will shape the next clinical governance standard. Until the third edition is released and assessment against it begins, services are assessed against the second edition actions described on this page.
